author: Doctor
text:
Look at the daily chart. The daily takes priority over lower time frames and it should have been obvious to anyone trading this pair that the lower price target for pro money bullish activity was where this was going. Further guidance was given from there being an old decision area to the left, proven bullish orders to the left which we were about to enter for the first time since that move, and we also were gaining support from those old bullish orders too.

There was little to be gained by pro money to take this lower, look where all the buying and selling took place below the last few days. Who would want to sell into that with the world and their granny already in major bearish mode.

For their to be any downside we have to push price up first in order to get enough margin and cheapest price to enter. I saw neither for a bearish move a few days back and was not willing to take a bearish position no matter what time frame or position size it could have been.

Even looking at the chart now, we have more attractive targets above that are showing very good old price action as well.

You should keep the big picture in mind all the time, even if this is the monthly and daily.

People who trade with real money and who take positions for months see this picture better than most can. But if you keep the same picture in your head and know the direction, all you want is a few good opportunities on lower time frames to trade in the same direction as they do. GBP/USD has only had its 4th entry for longer term positional traders (investors in reality) this year. Average moves were 800 points.

I obtain the same points gain and a lot more most of the time on lower time frames by watching what they are doing and by scaling into positions as the market shows me the real direction and over all I gain the same points gained.

I mentioned this in the past and its worth mentioning again. If you trade sure supply and demand it is unlikely you will become successful as you could. The reason is when the market turns based on those who matter i.e longer term pro money, it will break everything you ever read about supply and demand trading.

You will eventually learn to spot this by making three observations:

1. Big Picture

2. Big Picture

3. Big Picture

There is also a fundamental reason why supply and demand trading fails in its classic description around these turning areas. Pro money cannot bail out of and get into a position in one hit. They have to scale in and out and this takes time. If they just jumped in and out all the time, what you would see is incredibly long wicks and tails on price action. The violence these create will break your account in minutes and destroy how the markets now move. What they do is filter money in and out of the market in smaller bites. These smaller bites are shown as periods of consolidation on lower time frames. You can rest assured pro money is active when the market appears dull, but it must be within a generally active market such as London or New York. We are dealing with the best financial brains on the planet and they know how the herd reacts. If too much money is placed or withdrawn from the market the price will move against the pro's too quickly and their investors will not be happy. They have price orders to fill and price is always king, and so is their fee if they get it right.

A safer way to trade is to wait a few days after the daily/weekly turn has established a new direction because people have spent a lift time trying to pick tops and bottoms.

I trust this has shown you that focusing on supply and demand on the lower time frame will throw you off the main market sentiment. Commit it to memory and look for it, it will be an eye opener and it will put you in the same place where the rich and even richer make their money.

author: Doctor
text:
I will scale in early and also scale out early depending on how the price action looks. There are a number of ways you can look at the market depending on your capital, time in the trade and target(s).

The higher time frames generally spend more time to unwind the current direction and slow down the move, then start applying positions in the opposite direction, which means pro money will be buying all of the bearish orders in this example, if they buy enough of the sellers orders they stop the momentum going down and the market will consolidate for a time, this provides them with excellent long grass in which to load up in the direction they wish to go and not show their true intentions for some time, anything from hours, days and sometimes, weeks. The best you can hope for is to be aware of the price area where this is going on, and you will only see the effect after the fact. But that is good enough. Nobody can ever pin point the exact price where a market will turn.

There is no right way to scale in or out, my own approach is to slowly filter into the market the amount of capital I want to put into a move, but I break it down into smaller lot sizes and only apply new positions as I see entry signals on lower time frames. If I want to put in 10,000 euro, I could use 100 lots at one time, but its too risk. Instead I may put in 5 or 10 lots at a time, and over a period of time and eventually get the full amount of capital I have decided to use for the move into the market in a some what covert manner.

Another approach is to only add positions when the new direction is obvious to everyone and only take them when old demand i.e the first new new demand created out of what looks like it should have been supply, is tested and support proven. These areas I prefer to see tested after a 4hr candle close, this is a safer way than taking them off the 5min, 15min and 1 hr. There are cycles within a pull back and the deeper ones tend to bring more profit because it is a very low cost way for pro money to get you out, take your money and run back in the direction you had correctly chosen.

Before you take to scaling into and out of positions, master conventional entries and exists. There are plenty more trades out there and missing one is no big deal, in fact trades are like buses, there will be another coming along real soon.

text:
Brilliant reponse Doc

As always a great source of learning. This thread is going to be considered for years as a classic text. A real credit to this site and to every trader reading.

Anyway, enough of that!:)

I've been reading an interesting thread over at Forex Factory called 'Technical Analysis Fallacy' which discusses an 'art of war' trading style of edging into the market with a small position (scout) and then sending in the troops once the move is confirmed.

The trader (fti) recommends trading without a stop loss so he cannot be shunted out of a position. If a trade goes against him he talks about adding rescue positions by averaging into the losing position and then taking some positions out as the trade recovers direction.

Although this sounds like a very dangerous way to trade it makes sense in a lot of ways. I'm not sure using rigid fixed pip stop or hiding stops in ridiculous places such as behind swing lows is such a good idea, as I've learned the hard way. I should have been in this GBPUSD position but got wrong footed and lost a fair amount of capital in the process.

author: Doctor
text:
It brings a good feeling people are getting something out of this. We all know that the day will also come when this will be no more. Life is a strange game.

If you are in a loosing position and you hedge against it, you'd better have deep pockets. That is a technique used by the foolish traders to offset losses. It is done by weak hands and those who wont close out and want to save face. If I have a bad trade, I take the hit and move on and will not throw good money after bad by doing what is to the vast majority of traders to be a bad move.

What you will see happen is for a trade in the wrong direction closed, and immediately placed back on in the opposite direction. If you do the math with say 2 trades in the wrong direction and now two more in the correct direction, at all are equal value lots, there is no way you will offset a loss. You have to trade with more money against the first trades. That is plain silly in my book.

When I can sit and watch the market move and I place a trade, I will do so without a stop. If I cannot sit and manage the trade I will place a hard stop. But the mental stop I have in place NEVER moves and it is the end of a trade with no if/and or but.

If you dont have the capital to trade longer term but still want higher points made, you can trade with partial lots and sit there and watch it move enough to gain some safety as each successive time frame pulls back and gives you more space between your entry price and current price. My longer term trades will hide behind support in the case of a move up, and behind resistance on the way down. I wont put them a point behind it, but well behind it because a weekly open can produce a gap or a strong fast and fake move to stop you out. All this is designed by pro money, however the higher time frame picture will play out. It just needs for you to give it the time and space it needs to move.

The market is now open and what will we expect with the GBP/USD pair?.....a move down would nice, into support, bounce off and then continue on in the direction chosen last week. Day traders will have a bad day tomorrow I think.
